title: Running Middle Value
statement:
Numbers arrive one at a time. At any moment you may be asked for the median of all numbers so far: the middle value once they are sorted. With an even count there is no single middle value, so the median is the average of the two middle values.

  • MedianFinder() creates an empty collection.
  • addNum(num) adds the integer num.
  • findMedian() returns the median of everything added so far, as a floating-point number. It is only called after at least one addNum.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the collection. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned). Since the inputs are integers, every median is a whole number or ends in .5.

examples.why: With two numbers the median is (−2 + 8) / 2 = 3. With three it is the middle one after sorting, −2, 5, 8 → 5, not the middle one in arrival order (−2).
Medians can end in .5. After 10 and 3 arrive, the sorted values are 1, 3, 4, 10, and the middle pair is 3 and 4.

constraints: findMedian is only called after at least one addNum
hints: Keeping everything sorted makes findMedian easy but addNum slow. Do you need the whole order, or only the values near the middle?
Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. The median depends only on the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half.
Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, with the lower half equal in size or one larger. Each add goes into one heap, then one value moves across to restore the sizes.

explain.intuition:
The median only cares about the one or two values in the middle. So split everything seen so far into a lower half and an upper half, where every value in the lower half is ≤ every value in the upper half. Then the median is the largest of the lower half (when it has one extra value) or the average of the largest lower value and the smallest upper value. Those are exactly the tops of a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half.

Adding a number must keep both rules: every lower value ≤ every upper value, and the sizes equal or the lower half one bigger. A simple way: push the new number into the lower heap, then move the lower heap's top to the upper heap. The value that crossed is the largest of the lower half plus the new number, so the order rule holds. If the upper heap is now bigger, move its top back. Each add is a few O(log n) heap steps, and findMedian reads two tops in O(1). In Python, the lower half is a max-heap built from heapq by storing negated values.
steps: Keep low, a max-heap of the lower half, and high, a min-heap of the upper half.
addNum(x): push x into low, then pop low's top and push it into high.
If high now has more values than low, pop its top and push it back into low.
findMedian(): if low is bigger, return its top. Otherwise return (low.top + high.top) / 2.
pitfalls: Pushing a new value into whichever heap is smaller without comparing it to the tops. A large value can then land in the lower half and break the order rule.
In Python, forgetting that low holds negated values: reading low[0] instead of -low[0] flips the sign of the median.
Integer division for the even case. (3 + 4) // 2 is 3, but the median of 3 and 4 is 3.5.

complexity.time: O(log n) per addNum, O(1) per findMedian

solutions.title: Sort on every query
solutions.idea: Store all numbers. On findMedian, sort a copy and read the middle.
solutions.time: O(1) add, O(n log n) per query

solutions.title: Sorted array with binary-search insert
solutions.idea: Keep the numbers sorted at all times. Binary search finds the insert position, but shifting the later elements is still O(n).

solutions.title: Two heaps: lower half and upper half
solutions.idea: A max-heap holds the lower half and a min-heap the upper half, sizes balanced. The median is read from their tops.

followups: All numbers are between 0 and 100. How would you answer in O(1) per call without heaps?
Report the median of only the last w numbers, a sliding window. Why do plain heaps struggle with removals, and what can you do about it?
